description: We are HELIXE, a multidisciplinary team of medical and engineering students. We aim to create synergy between our ideas to develop a high-impact solution for health monitoring software for space missions. We are passionate about space health, human exploration, and technological development. We combine clinical precision and programming to protect the astronauts of the future.
summary:
ORBIOS is a web-based health monitoring prototype for astronauts, developed by the HELIXE team, designed to facilitate the tracking of physical well-being during long-duration space missions.
The project addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut health while they are far from medical teams on Earth. To achieve this, it integrates data on vital signs, sleep, fatigue, muscle performance, vision, and radiation exposure into a single dashboard. Its key innovation lies in comparing each astronaut’s measurements against their own personal baseline, identifying changes that may require attention. Furthermore, it incorporates artificial intelligence to interpret symptoms, visualize the affected areas of the body, and provide guidance on when to re-check a measurement or seek medical assistance.

ORBIOS is significant because it promotes greater autonomy and safety for astronauts, streamlines communication with ground-based medical teams, and contributes to the development of future health-monitoring technologies for space exploration. It is not intended to diagnose medical conditions, but rather to help detect changes in a timely manner and support informed decision-making.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

ORBIOS is a health monitoring system designed for astronauts on long-duration missions. It is based on a simple premise: in space, it is more useful to compare an individual against their own personal baseline rather than against a chart of “normal” values. Consequently, every measurement is evaluated relative to that person’s established baseline.

The process works as follows: incoming data, such as pulse, sleep, fatigue, strength, retinal scans, and signals from a biometric shirt are compared against the individual’s personal reference point. If a change persists, the app does not provide a diagnosis; instead, it prompts the astronaut to repeat the measurement, check the sensor, and record what they were doing at the time. A 3D model of the human body indicates which areas may require attention, and all this information is compiled into a summary ready to be sent to the medical team back on Earth.

The most prominent feature is the astronaut’s dashboard. Here, the user can select “Talk” to describe how they are feeling in their own words; the app transcribes this input, cross-references it with the collected data, and assesses the level of urgency and the appropriate next steps. Surrounding this dashboard are several modules:

Retinal monitoring (SANS), aligned with NASA’s clinical guidelines;

knee-repetition counting, utilizing the computer’s camera;

analysis of data from the biometric shirt (ECG, heart rate variability, and respiration);

real-world radiation data from the ISS and biomarker data from the Inspiration4 mission;

a knowledge map detailing what is currently understood about the human body in the environments of the Moon, Mars, and orbit.

What are the benefits?

The primary benefit is early detection. By comparing data against an individual’s own historical baseline, changes can be identified before they become clinically apparent. It also grants the astronaut greater autonomy, they know what to check without needing to wait for input from Earth, which is critical for a mission to Mars, where communication delays can span several minutes.

We have also ensured that the app does not trigger unnecessary alarms. Each reading indicates its origin and level of reliability; if any data is missing, we do not invent it. When the medical team needs to be alerted, the summary already includes the values, the quality of the readings, the actions taken by the astronaut, and the sources. Furthermore, it can be used via voice, text, or the camera no special equipment required. The video never leaves the browser, and the audio is not saved.

What is the expected impact?

We envision this being used for long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, where a doctor cannot respond instantly, requiring astronauts to make more decisions on their own. We also believe this concept has applications here on Earth such as at Antarctic research stations, in rural areas, or within telemedicine where individuals may be far from medical professionals. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NASA’s open data can be integrated into a tool that is intuitive for anyone to use, with clear attribution for the source of every piece of information.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did we use?

The application is built using TypeScript, Next.js 16, and React 19, allowing us to manage both the frontend and the server within a single project. For the user interface, we utilized Tailwind CSS, and for data visualization, we employed Recharts. The 3D representations of the human body and the solar system were created using three.js, incorporating anatomical models from BodyParts3D (licensed under CC BY 4.0). To track movement via the camera, we used MediaPipe, which runs directly in the browser.

We leveraged OpenAI models: `gpt-5.4-mini` for the "copilot" functionality and `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe` for speech-to-text conversion. Browser APIs, specifically MediaRecorder and Web Audio were used to record audio and detect when a user has finished speaking.

Data processing scripts for NASA datasets were written in Node.js. Additionally, we developed a Python script using ReportLab to generate the PDF documents reviewed by the medical team. The data is sourced from NASA’s OSDR (studies OSD-569 and OSD-575), RadLab, EDA, the Human Research Roadmap reports, the NASA-STD-3001 standard, and NASA’s guidance on SANS (Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome).

To ensure quality, we implemented 307 automated tests and validated the data using JSON Schema. We used GitHub for version control and Vercel for deployment. Throughout the development process, we utilized Claude Code as a programming assistant. In terms of hardware, we don’t need anything special: we work using our computers, a webcam, and a microphone. The app is designed for use with smart shirts like Astroskin or Bio-Monitor, though for now, data is loaded from CSV or JSON files.

In what sense is it creative?

What we like most about the project is that it avoids making diagnoses. Instead of telling someone what condition they might have, it explains what has changed relative to their own baseline and what might be worth checking. The 3D model of the body follows this same principle: it highlights areas to look at, rather than claiming that a specific organ is damaged.

We also bring together, on a single screen, elements that are usually kept separate: voice, camera input, vital signs, retinal data, and information from the biometric shirt. Furthermore, we can assess muscle status using only a webcam without the need for external sensors or recording any video.

We have set clear boundaries for the AI. It only receives the data we provide; if it fabricates a number, attempts to make a diagnosis, or recommends a treatment, we discard that response. If the AI ​​is unavailable, the app continues to function, providing an assessment based solely on the raw measurements.

What factors did we take into account?

First and foremost was safety. ORBIOS does not provide diagnoses, issue prescriptions, or independently determine whether a situation is urgent. Warning signs such as chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting—are always detected based on specific keywords, ensuring they are identified even if the AI ​​fails.

Secondly, we relied on evidence. Every rule cites the specific NASA report it is based on including the page number and also clarifies what the report does not support. The rules and text were reviewed by medical experts across four specialties: internal medicine, neurology, aerospace medicine, and general medicine.

We were also careful with the data. The data for the demo subject, "DEMO-01," was generated by our team; actual NASA data is always displayed separately and never mixed in. If a measurement is missing, we do not attempt to fill it in. We considered the conditions of an actual mission: communication delays, the limited time available to the crew, and the need for an easy-to-read display. For this reason, the interface features high contrast and can be operated via keyboard, screen reader, or voice commands.

We are aware of the limitations. We have not yet tested the camera with real people, and in this demo, data is not saved between sessions. This is a hackathon prototype it is neither a medical device nor endorsed by NASA.
